When Maryland reduced avoidable hospital admissions, the reduction was concentrated among healthier patients — people who, with adequate primary care and social support, would not have needed hospitalization. The sickest patients continued arriving at emergency departments, and hospitals actually spent more time treating them.

Maryland’s experience complicates the simple story. Hospitals reported that avoidable use was hardest to reduce among patients with complex needs, even though the federal evaluation found the largest Medicare reductions among dual-eligible beneficiaries and those with multiple chronic conditions — and the same evaluation found no improvement in population health.
